projects.title: Mode/s of Making
projects.subtitle: Heat rotate cutting
projects.summary: My studio study connects rotary heat cutting, custom polystyrene units and the textures left by fabrication.
projects.metadataDescription: A studio study connecting rotary heat cutting, custom polystyrene units, machine design and physical surface prototypes.
projects.context: National Cheng Kung University · Tainan, Taiwan
projects.role: Studio design research - computational design and fabrication workflow

hero.alt: Curvature-parameter assembly simulation from the original studio film.
hero.caption: Curvature-parameter assembly simulation from the original studio film.
hero.credit: Studio design and digital animation: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Start with the making process.
paragraphs: I explored rotary heat cutting as a design tool, using the movement of the cutter to shape polystyrene units. The fabrication mechanism became part of the design process.
The unit geometry and its possible assemblies developed together, linking digital configurations with physical surface studies.

media.alt: Original unit-geometry animation from the studio film materials.
media.caption: Original unit-geometry animation from the studio film materials.
media.credit: Studio design and digital animation: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Coordinate tool and workpiece.
paragraphs: The system combines planar tool movement with a rotating workpiece. The original CoreXY animation shows the motion frame, motors and carriage as a coordinated mechanism.
I connected geometry development, cutting-path optimisation, G-code conversion and machine setup in a design-to-fabrication workflow, using Arduino and Marlin as control foundations.

media.alt: CoreXY movement study from the original studio animation.
media.caption: CoreXY movement study from the original studio animation.
media.credit: Studio design and digital animation: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: A machine for the study.
paragraphs: The machine study combines a CoreXY-style motion frame with a rotating holder for the polystyrene blank. Motors, rods, belts and bearings coordinate the relationship between tool and workpiece.
The original studio animation brings the machine and rotating blank together; the film diagram distinguishes its rotating area from the working area.

media.alt: Rotating area and working area in the film's digital machine study.
media.caption: Rotating area and working area in the film's digital machine study.
media.credit: Studio design and digital animation: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Fabrication
sections.title: Watch the tool meet the material.
paragraphs: The studio film records a physical heat-cutting operation at the tool and foam interface. The selected excerpt shows the heated tip and polystyrene in contact as the cut develops.
My workflow connected the cutting profile and machine setup with material trials. This recorded operation brings the mechanism back to the surface it produces.

media.alt: Physical heat-cutting operation from the original studio film.
media.caption: Physical heat-cutting operation from the original studio film.
media.credit: Studio design and fabrication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Cutting
sections.title: Follow the prototype in operation.
paragraphs: A separate workshop recording shows the built prototype cutting a mounted polystyrene workpiece. The shaped blank rotates between its holders while the heated cutting tool engages the surface.
The view makes the relationship between machine movement, the changing profile and the resulting texture visible at the scale of a single unit.

media.alt: Original recording of the physical rotary-cutting prototype machining a polystyrene workpiece.
media.caption: Original recording of the physical rotary-cutting prototype machining a polystyrene workpiece.
media.credit: Studio design and fabrication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Connect the unit to the workflow.
paragraphs: The original studio film connects the layered unit and cutting profile to a workflow from geometry development through cutting-path optimisation and G-code conversion.
I used the relationship between toolpaths and custom units to explore how fabrication can inform an assembly design.

media.alt: The studio film connects a layered unit and cutting profile with the design-to-code workflow.
media.caption: Recorded design-to-code workflow and unit cutting-profile study from the original studio film.
media.credit: Studio design and digital animation: Chia-Hsuan Chao / National Cheng Kung University.

projects.sourceNote: I developed the studio design by connecting the cutting mechanism, unit geometry, toolpaths and assembly configurations. The fabrication workflow uses Arduino, Marlin and a customised motion frame; Prof. Kane Yanagawa supervised the studio.

projects.title: Entrance Installation Art
projects.subtitle: Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square
projects.summary: I helped turn a patterned entrance installation into coordinated 3D models and fabrication drawings within the PKD engineering team.
projects.metadataDescription: Scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication-drawing coordination for the Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square entrance installation.

hero.alt: View upward along the completed installation, with folded triangular metal panels and openings.
hero.caption: The folded panel surface of the Taichung Nan Shan no.6 Square entrance installation.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: From a surface to individual panels.
paragraphs: I worked within the PKD team to develop an entrance installation from a continuous surface into individually defined folded panels.
The design connected the overall form with a practical system of openings, edges and supports that could be carried into fabrication.

media.alt: Four digital models progress from a smooth surface to triangulation, depth and openings.
media.caption: Surface subdivision, panel depth and a helical distance field develop the pattern.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

media.alt: A grid of related installation models compares different panel opening patterns.
media.caption: Pattern schemes developed within the same overall installation geometry.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Control variation through geometry.
paragraphs: My modelling work connected the triangulated surface with panel depth, opening patterns and a shared reference system. These relationships let local variation remain coordinated with the overall installation.
The model and drawings developed together so that each panel could be identified and related to its neighbours.

media.alt: Section and joint illustrations show the support frame and two-ear and three-ear folded panels.
media.caption: The support system and the two families of folded panel connections.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Translate the model for fabrication.
paragraphs: I translated the 3D panel geometry into fabrication drawings, bringing together fold angles, holes, tabs and reference information.
Model-derived information and manual checks were coordinated with the fabrication team. The physical modules were fabricated in the workshop and assembled by the project team.

media.alt: Flat panel drawings retain fold lines, holes, dimensions and folding-angle information.
media.caption: The model is translated into dimensioned fabrication drawings for individual panels.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

media.alt: Workshop photographs show internal supports and the installation modules during fabrication.
media.caption: Workshop documentation of the internal supports and separately fabricated modules.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Read the assembled geometry.
paragraphs: The completed surface brings the variation of individual openings into a continuous entrance installation. Close views reveal folds, edges and the relationship between neighbouring panels.
My contribution covered scheme development, 3D modelling and fabrication drawings within the wider engineering, fabrication and installation team.

media.alt: Photographs show the completed installation, close panel details and its urban setting.
media.caption: Built surface details and the entrance installation in its site context.
media.credit: Project: PKD Engineering Consultants.

credits.role: Scheme development, modelling and fabrication drawings

projects.title: Dot-Based 3D Printing
projects.subtitle: Printing Architecture · Dot-based non-planar fabrication
projects.summary: I explored printing parameters and toolpath delays with Group1 to develop dotted surfaces across different geometries.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team project exploring dot-based non-planar printing through parameter samples, deposition strategies and physical prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
projects.role: Printing research - computational toolpaths and physical experimentation with Group1

hero.alt: A translucent twisted printed object stands in snow against grass and trees.
hero.caption: A physical prototype from the dot-based non-planar printing study.
hero.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Parameters become material patterns.
paragraphs: I explored layer height, density, speed and pattern settings through printed samples with Group1. The surfaces reveal how those choices change bead spacing and texture.
We then carried the dotted surface language from small samples into curved and twisted geometries.

media.alt: A parameter diagram and twelve printed samples compare dotted and continuous textures.
media.caption: Layer height, density, pattern and speed are explored through a family of printed samples.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Coordinate paths and delays.
paragraphs: I worked on the relationship between robotic paths and deposition delays as part of our printing study. Different combinations of movement and material placement produced smooth and dotted regions.
Path studies and printed samples connect the motion strategy with the texture that appears in the material.

media.alt: Three path diagrams are paired with printed rings and close views of deposited beads.
media.caption: Different deposition paths and time-delay strategies produce different bead patterns.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

media.alt: Three printed shapes are paired with digital line models of their increasingly twisted geometries.
media.caption: The printing strategy is explored across a sequence of different overall forms.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Watch the pattern being deposited.
paragraphs: The nozzle deposits material along the specimen edge, building the dotted pattern through the relationship between motion and extrusion.
Our printing experiments connected parameter studies with physical trials on different overall forms.

media.alt: A printing nozzle deposits material along the upper edge of a dotted specimen.
media.caption: A still frame from the original Group1 fabrication recording.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: A family of physical experiments.
paragraphs: The prototypes explore different twists and overall shapes while retaining visible patterns in the deposited material.
A translucent TPU prototype family extends the study into a lit display, where light reveals the bead structure and variation between surfaces.

media.alt: Three white printed objects compare different degrees of twist and bead pattern.
media.caption: The physical geometry-development prototypes.
media.credit: Group1 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Namdev Talluru / JunJie.

media.alt: A group of translucent printed objects is lit from below, revealing their surface patterns.
media.caption: The translucent TPU prototype family in a lit display.

projects.title: HC3DP Caustics
projects.subtitle: Inflation-based Pattern Exploration
projects.summary: I explored computational printing paths, inflated shells and their light patterns as part of Group-Red.
projects.metadataDescription: A Group-Red study of inflated printed shells, computational paths and photographed caustic light patterns.
projects.role: Computational design and fabrication research with Group-Red

hero.alt: Transparent printed shells stand on a table, with light passing through their inflated surfaces.
hero.caption: Physical shells from the Group-Red inflation and caustics study.
hero.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: Inflated shells and light.
paragraphs: I explored complex caustic patterns through simple shell geometries with Group-Red, drawing on Greek meander motifs and the Hilbert curve.
The study combined pattern changes within each layer with planar layer addition, connecting the printing strategy with the form of the shell.

media.alt: An original diagram pairs the printing tool and inflated shell with three parallel point rows.
media.caption: The original layer-slicing and curve-division diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Paths and frames.
paragraphs: I worked on the computational path study as part of the team. We divided layers into bottom, middle and top point rows and used the connections between them to define the printing path.
Frame arrangement and tilt became part of the computational workflow for guiding the tool along that path.

media.alt: An original diagram connects points across three rows below the printing-tool model.
media.caption: The original diagram of connections between bottom, middle and top point rows.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

media.alt: An original diagram places tilted coordinate frames along a printing path.
media.caption: The original frame-arrangement diagram.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Connect a path with material behaviour.
paragraphs: The fabrication-path animation brings the tool, shell geometry and path frames together as a simulation of the printing strategy.
Our physical experiments were sensitive to air pressure and cooling. Adjusting the process meant working with the material as well as the digital path.

media.alt: A printing-path simulation frame shows the tool and a row of red path frames.
media.caption: A still from the original fabrication-path animation; this is a simulation.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: Observe the light and the failures.
paragraphs: The printed geometries produced different light patterns, which we studied through physical experiments.
Sticking and overinflation were also part of the investigation. The curved orange samples show how the material can depart from the intended shell geometry.

media.alt: A translucent printed form creates a radiating light pattern on a wall.
media.caption: A photographed caustic pattern produced during the project experiments.
media.credit: Group-Red: Paul Jaeggi / Behnur Baiju / Kevin Seav / JosHsuan Chao.

media.caption: Overinflation deforms the curved shell samples.

projects.title: Special Assemblies
projects.subtitle: V-Shape Modular Based Aggregation
projects.summary: I worked with Kevin Seav and Megi Sinani to explore reciprocal V-shaped stick modules and robotic assembly planning.
projects.metadataDescription: A 2023 ETH MAS DFab team study connecting V-shaped stick aggregation with robot trajectories and physical assembly prototypes.
projects.context: MAS DFab, ETH Zurich · Zurich, Switzerland
projects.role: Computational geometry and robotic-assembly research with Group6

hero.alt: A curved assembly of wooden sticks rises from a small base beside a robotic arm.

hero.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A reciprocal starting point.
paragraphs: I explored V-shaped wooden-stick modules with Kevin Seav and Megi Sinani, drawing on reciprocal structures. Each addition changes the relationships between neighbouring sticks.
Physical prototypes connected this bottom-up geometric study with the conditions of robotic assembly.

media.alt: An early wooden-stick aggregation cantilevers from a small dome-shaped foundation.
media.caption: A physical study of the reciprocal stick aggregation and its foundation.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani.

sections.label: System
sections.title: Rules guide the next module.
paragraphs: I worked on the geometric aggregation study as part of Group6. We organised directional growth into four choices: NE, NW, SE and SW, and explored module relationships through an object-oriented model.
The workflow connected geometry and assembly data with ROS/MoveIt planning through JSON, simulation and replanning.

media.alt: Module diagrams and sequential stick assemblies show four directional aggregation choices.
media.caption: The original VStickModule and directional-aggregation diagrams, with their figure captions.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Project diagram.

media.caption: The original software and JSON-based robotic planning workflow.
media.credit: Group6 project: Chia-Hsuan Chao / Kevin Seav / Megi Sinani. Project diagram.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: Plan the assembly sequence.
paragraphs: Pick, place, exit and insert trajectories organised robot movement around the growing structure.
We studied stick ordering and tool-frame direction, including a Z-axis correction intended to reduce gripper interference with the table.

media.alt: A robotic assembly diagram labels pick, approach, safe, place and exit frames around the stick prototype.
media.caption: The recorded pick, place, exit and insert trajectory stages for V-stick aggregation.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: From modules to a prototype.
paragraphs: The physical assembly brings the accumulated stick relationships into view from the front and above.
The prototypes connect reciprocal aggregation with the practical task of placing the next stick in an increasingly complex arrangement.

projects.title: Project Caschlatsch
projects.subtitle: Timber fabrication and AR assembly
projects.summary: I worked on computational design and XR production tools within the collective timber-tower project, connecting beam aggregation, digital fabrication and assembly.
projects.metadataDescription: Timber fabrication and AR-guided module assembly, with COMPAS XR feature development.
projects.role: Computational design and COMPAS XR development - ETH MAS DFab 2023-24 cohort project

hero.alt: Timber tower model on a stepped white site model in front of a window.
hero.caption: The architectural timber-tower model.
hero.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: Context
sections.title: A collective timber tower.
paragraphs: Project Caschlatsch brought the MAS DFab cohort together around a modular timber structure, connecting computational design, fabrication and assembly. The project developed at ETH Zurich and became a built installation at Disentis/Mustér.

We worked across a shared digital model, prefabricated timber modules and collaborative assembly. Within this collective project, my work connected computational design with the XR tools used during production.

media.alt: Timber tower seen through trees with visitors gathered at its base.
media.caption: The constructed timber tower on site.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: System
sections.title: From voxels to a beam system.
paragraphs: I worked on the cohort's voxel-to-beam aggregation in Python and Grasshopper. We used spatial cells to keep beam placement tied to indexed positions and neighbouring cells, so the timber modules grew through explicit geometric rules.

The shared framework separated processing from geometry: ID managed voxel indexing and neighbour relationships, while Discrete Vector Generator supplied candidate directions. Voxel represented spatial cells, Beam the timber elements, and Layer groups of voxels.
A 26-direction discretisation converted this spatial map into beam axes through voxel centres. Stored voxel data tracked existing beams to control new intersections and avoid redundant crossings.

The module strategy combined an edge frame with orthogonal and diagonal supports, then varied the beam infill. Five-beam and 30-beam configurations explored different densities within that common frame.

My code work included separating the aggregation solver and ID/vector tools for Grasshopper, and refining occupied-voxel checks for the flying-beam problem. This development was part of the shared research that connected aggregation, module planning and fabrication.

media.alt: Original diagram of ID and Discrete Vector Generator processing classes and Voxel, Beam and Layer geometry classes.
media.caption: The original five-class framework for voxel-based structural generation.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

media.alt: Original voxel module studies showing initial frames, orthogonal and diagonal support, and five- and thirty-beam infill.
media.caption: Module-frame, orthogonal/diagonal support and 5-/30-beam infill strategies (upper schematic detail).
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: XR guidance

media.caption: The original AR-based beam and module assembly sequence.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

media.alt: Original CAD-to-Firebase-to-AR diagram with JSON building plans/checklists and OBJ mesh data.
media.caption: The original cloud data-exchange framework for XR and CAD.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

media.alt: Original annotated assembly app interfaces identifying orientation, float, scale, module rotation and selection, beam ID, sequence order and stacking/assembly modes.
media.caption: The original XR interfaces for modular assembly and beam positioning.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.title: Developing XR for multi-module assembly.
paragraphs: During production, I improved COMPAS XR so users could select and switch assembly modules from a cloud server, track beam IDs and follow the assembly sequence in real time. The current module, selected beam and sequence step kept the interface tied to the component being assembled.

The shared workflow began with a COMPAS Timber assembly plan. Building plans and checklists were serialised as JSON, with OBJ files carrying mesh geometry. Firebase connected this CAD data to the AR applications, which retrieved and deserialised it for use beside the physical work.

The project's assembly and stacking applications supported different workshop tasks. Beam selection, orientation arrows and a floating-beam view helped inspect a component and its cutting features; scaling, three-axis rotation and stacking/assembly modes supported module inspection and positioning.

I also worked on the Rhino-to-COMPAS data preparation, including converting stacking planes into frames and preparing module building-plan and mesh exports. My multi-module and sequence-interface development sat within this collaborative CAD, cloud and XR production system.

sections.label: Making
sections.title: One model, many hands.
paragraphs: The digital model connected beam geometry with fabrication and module assembly. Robotic and CNC processes prepared timber elements, while students worked together to assemble the modules.

The workshop brought digital planning into contact with physical handling and coordination. XR guidance was one part of that shared making process, alongside the people, tools and prefabricated components.

media.caption: XR-guided timber assembly in the collaborative workshop.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

media.alt: Industrial robot and people working around a timber assembly in the fabrication workshop.
media.caption: Robot-assisted timber module assembly.
media.credit: Source publication: Chia-Hsuan Chao / ETH MAS DFab 2023–24.

sections.label: Results
sections.title: From modules to a place.
paragraphs: The assembled modules create a route through the timber interior, with steps rising toward a lookout. Repeated beams form both the structure and the experience of moving through it.
The completed installation is a cohort and partner achievement. It brings computational aggregation, digital fabrication and collaborative assembly together in a place that can be entered and used.
